<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A1.SS0.SSS0.Px7" title="In Appendix A Formal Definitions of Baseline Samplers ‣ Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Block Diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<span class="ltx_ref">Arriola et al., 2025</span>; <span class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025b</span>)</cite></span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A2" title="In Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B </span>Detailed Hyperparameter Settings</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A3" title="In Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">C </span>Theoretical Analysis of the Info-Gain Objective</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">

<article class="ltx_document ltx_pruned_first">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Kaisen Yang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University.<span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">yks23@mails.tsinghua.edu</span>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jayden Teoh
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Singapore Management University,
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Kaicheng Yang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Shanghaijiaotong University
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yitong Zhang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Beihang University
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Alex Lamb
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>College of AI, Tsinghua University
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">alex6200@gmail.com</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) offer greater flexibility in decoding order than autoregressive models but require careful planning to achieve high-quality generation. Existing samplers typically adopt greedy heuristics, prioritizing positions with the highest local certainty to decode at each step. Through failure case analysis, we identify a fundamental limitation of this approach: it neglects the downstream impact of current decoding choices on subsequent steps and fails to minimize cumulative uncertainty. In particular, these methods do not fully exploit the non-causal nature of MDMs, which enables evaluating how a decoding decision reshapes token probabilities/uncertainty across all remaining masked positions. To bridge this gap, we propose the <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Info-Gain Sampler</span>, a principled decoding framework that balances immediate uncertainty with information gain over future masked tokens.
Extensive evaluations across diverse architectures and tasks (reasoning, coding, creative writing, and image generation) demonstrate that Info-Gain Sampler consistently outperforms existing samplers for MDMs. For instance, it achieves a 3.6% improvement in average accuracy on reasoning tasks and a 63.1% win-rate in creative writing. Notably, on reasoning tasks it reduces cumulative uncertainty from 78.4 to 48.6, outperforming the best baseline by a large margin. The code will be available at <a href="https://github.com/yks23/Information-Gain-Sampler" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/yks23/Information-Gain-Sampler</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to the dominant autoregressive paradigm for discrete sequence generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lou et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. By leveraging bidirectional attention, MDMs break free from strict left-to-right generation, granting unprecedented flexibility in decoding paths <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. This flexibility unlocks superior performance in tasks requiring bidirectional attention, such as code infilling, biological sequence design, and long-horizon planning tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, this potential remains largely untapped due to a training–inference mismatch. While MDMs are trained under random masking patterns, inference entails a multi-step, order-sensitive decoding process. Navigating the large space of possible decoding orders therefore requires a sampler that carefully selects which tokens to reveal next. Consequently, generation quality is heavily dependent on the effectiveness of the sampler <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing samplers predominantly rely on <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">local certainty heuristics</span> such as confidence to greedily select the next decoding target <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. In Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Motivation ‣ 3 Method ‣ Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we argue and demonstrate that such samplers are often nonrobust due to the myopia of local heuristics: they ignore the long-term impact of current decoding decisions on future uncertainty. Consequently, they frequently prioritize tokens that appear syntactically <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">confident</span> but are semantically suboptimal, leading to error propagation and compromised generation quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to autoregressive models (ARMs), where the causal nature makes evaluating the downstream effect of a token choice computationally prohibitive, the bidirectional nature of MDMs offers a distinct advantage: it enables us to assess how a token decoding decision influences the uncertainty across all remaining masked positions immediately.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Leveraging these insights, we propose the <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Information Gain (Info-Gain) Sampler</span>, a decoding framework that departs from greedy certainty-based sampling. Instead of merely refining the certainty scoring function, the Info-Gain Sampler additionally evaluates decoding actions by how much they reduce the uncertainty in remaining masked tokens. By balancing <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">immediate certainty</span> with <span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">information gain</span>, our method prioritizes globally informative decisions and yields more robust decoding trajectories. Our contributions are threefold:</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F1.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:169.1pt;"><img src="2602.18176v1/illustrative.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:234/119;" width="234" height="119" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering">(a) The dilemma of greedy certainty-based sampling.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F1.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:169.1pt;"><img src="2602.18176v1/toy1-v4.png" id="S1.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:234/124;" width="234" height="124" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering">(b) Evolution of cumulative uncertainty.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Motivation:</span> Analysis of decoding strategies on the one-way multiplication experiment.
(a) Illustrates the contrast between the suboptimal path chosen by the greedy certainty-based sampler and the optimal path, motivating the introduction of the Info-Gain Sampler.
(b) Shows the evolution of cumulative uncertainty throughout the decoding process.
While the greedy sampler prioritizes decoding <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> first (73.2%) due to its immediate high confidence, it leads to failure because of the task’s one-way nature.
In contrast, the Info-Gain Sampler optimizes global uncertainty by resolving high-entropy factors <math id="S1.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> first (84.0%), ensuring a successful decoding trajectory.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">(1) We empirically identify the fundamental limitations of existing greedy certainty-based samplers in MDMs through failure case analyses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">(2) We introduce the Info-Gain Sampler, which balances immediate costs with future information gain via a simple yet effective objective. We also propose computationally efficient implementations of Info-Gain Sampler.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">(3) We extensively evaluate Info-Gain Sampler against other sampler baselines across diverse pretrained MDMs and benchmarks. The results show that Info-Gain consistently outperforms these baselines across math, coding, planning, writing, and image generation tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminary</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs)</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider discrete data over a vocabulary of size <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> with sequence length <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,\ldots,\mathcal{V}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\ldots,\mathcal{V}\}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the vocabulary, and let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> represent the special mask token. A state is denoted as <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}\in\{0,1,\ldots,\mathcal{V}\}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}\in\{0,1,\ldots,\mathcal{V}\}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> for discrete time steps <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0,1,\ldots,T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0,1,\ldots,T</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}^{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}^{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> is the token at position <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>. The data distribution <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{data}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>data</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{data}}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined over fully unmasked sequences in <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,\ldots,m\}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\ldots,m\}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, corresponding to <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Forward process.</span>
The forward process gradually corrupts a clean data point <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}\sim p_{\text{data}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>data</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}\sim p_{\text{data}}</annotation></semantics></math> by independently masking each coordinate over <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> steps. At each step, tokens are progressively replaced by the mask token <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> according to a fixed schedule, such that at time <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, the state is fully masked, i.e., <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{T}=(0,\ldots,0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{T}=(0,\ldots,0)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reverse process and training.</span>
To generate samples, we learn to reverse this forward process. A denoising network <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> predicts, for each masked position <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, the distribution of the original token <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}^{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}^{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>. The model is trained by minimizing the evidence lower bound, which reduces to a weighted cross-entropy loss over masked positions. As revealed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, this loss weights all possible infilling problems equally, meaning the optimal <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> learns to predict any masked token given any context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sampling.</span>
Sampling starts from the fully masked state <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{T}=(0,\ldots,0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{T}=(0,\ldots,0)</annotation></semantics></math>. At each step <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> (going backwards from <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>), given current state <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model computes distributions <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math> for all masked positions <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{t}:=\{\ell\mid z_{t}^{\ell}=0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{t}:=\{\ell\mid z_{t}^{\ell}=0\}</annotation></semantics></math> in a single forward pass.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sampler</span> <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> determines how to use these distributions to produce the next state <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Unlike autoregressive models where the sampler decides the next token at a fixed position, a sampler for MDMs decides which masked positions to fill and what tokens to assign. Specifically, it selects a subset <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to unmask and, for each <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\in A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\in A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, assigns a token <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{x}^{\ell}\sim p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><mo>∼</mo><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{x}^{\ell}\sim p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> (optionally with temperature scaling or top-<math id="S2.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> filtering). This yields an action <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}:=\{(\ell,\hat{x}^{\ell})\mid\ell\in A_{t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}:=\{(\ell,\hat{x}^{\ell})\mid\ell\in A_{t}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Applying <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> produces <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t-1}=\textsc{Apply}(z_{t},a_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Apply</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t-1}=\textsc{Apply}(z_{t},a_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, where each selected position is filled and all others remain unchanged. This process repeats until reaching <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, yielding a fully generated sequence <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,m\}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,m\}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Certainty-based samplers.</span>
A widely used family of samplers follows a two-stage procedure at each step. First, <span id="S2.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">token sampling</span>: for each masked position <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\in\mathcal{M}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\in\mathcal{M}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, draw a candidate token <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{x}^{\ell}\sim p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><mo>∼</mo><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{x}^{\ell}\sim p_{\theta}^{\ell}(\cdot|z_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>. Second, <span id="S2.SS1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">position selection</span>: select which positions to actually unmask using a <span id="S2.SS1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">certainty score</span> <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(\ell,z_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(\ell,z_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> that measures the model’s confidence at position <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>. Common choices for <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> include the top-1 probability of the predictive distribution (confidence), the negative entropy of the predictive distribution, or the margin between the top-2 probabilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. A formal description of mainstream certainty-based samplers is provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Formal Definitions of Baseline Samplers ‣ Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.
Given a time-dependent budget <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (the number of positions to unmask at step <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, determined by a predefined scheduling function), the sampler selects the subset <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> that maximizes total certainty:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}^{*}=\underset{A_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{t},|A_{t}|=K_{t}}{\mathrm{argmax}}\sum_{\ell\in A_{t}}\phi(\ell,z_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mi>argmax</mi><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.700em">A</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">t</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.700em">⊆</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">ℳ</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">t</mi></msub></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">|</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.700em">A</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">t</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">=</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.700em">K</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}^{*}=\underset{A_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{t},|A_{t}|=K_{t}}{\mathrm{argmax}}\sum_{\ell\in A_{t}}\phi(\ell,z_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.2" class="ltx_p">The final action is then <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}^{*}=\{(\ell,\hat{x}^{\ell})\mid\ell\in A_{t}^{*}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}^{*}=\{(\ell,\hat{x}^{\ell})\mid\ell\in A_{t}^{*}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. This ”most certain first” strategy fills positions where the model is most confident, leaving harder decisions for later steps when more context is available.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing certainty-based sampling methods typically employ a greedy strategy. These methods aim to minimize error accumulation by prioritizing the most certain positions. While this approach effectively reduces immediate uncertainty and enhances short-term reliability, it essentially performs a greedy optimization of the cumulative uncertainty. This leads us to a fundamental question:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS1.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="58.92" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 58.92" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,58.92) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#4040FF;" fill="#4040FF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 4.15 L 0 54.77 C 0 57.06 1.86 58.92 4.15 58.92 L 473.23 58.92 C 475.52 58.92 477.38 57.06 477.38 54.77 L 477.38 4.15 C 477.38 1.86 475.52 0 473.23 0 L 4.15 0 C 1.86 0 0 1.86 0 4.15 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2FF;" fill="#F2F2FF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 4.15 L 1.38 54.77 C 1.38 56.29 2.62 57.53 4.15 57.53 L 473.23 57.53 C 474.75 57.53 475.99 56.29 475.99 54.77 L 475.99 4.15 C 475.99 2.62 474.75 1.38 473.23 1.38 L 4.15 1.38 C 2.62 1.38 1.38 2.62 1.38 4.15 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 13.62 9.39)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:32.53em;--ltx-fo-height:3.09em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="45.51" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 42.82)" width="450.12"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S3.SS1.p2.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.53em;">
<span id="S3.SS1.p2.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Question 1:<span id="S3.SS1.p2.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Is greedy optimization closed to minimize cumulative uncertainty across steps?</span></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify the uncertainty throughout a generation process <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=z_{T}\rightarrow z_{T-1}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow z_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=z_{T}\rightarrow z_{T-1}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow z_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> , we first introduce
<span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cumulative Entropy</span> <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{H}</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> as a key metric, defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{H}(\tau):=\sum_{t=T}^{1}C(a_{t}\mid z_{t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">:=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></munderover><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{H}(\tau):=\sum_{t=T}^{1}C(a_{t}\mid z_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(a_{t}\mid z_{t})=\sum_{\ell\in A_{t}}H^{(\ell)}(z_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(a_{t}\mid z_{t})=\sum_{\ell\in A_{t}}H^{(\ell)}(z_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> represents the sum of marginal entropy for the tokens selected at step <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, given by the model’s output distribution. This metric quantifies the total uncertainty accumulated throughout the decoding trajectory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To explore this question, we present two case studies that illustrate the limitations of greedy samplers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Case Study 1: One-way Multiplication.</span>
The model is tasked with generating an equation <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a\times b=c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\times b=c</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> are decimal factors and <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is a binary product. This task is inherently one-way: computing a product from factors is straightforward, while factoring is not only computationally difficult but also particularly challenging for MDMs to generate, especially when the product is represented in binary format. Two decoding paths emerge: (i) <span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Product-first</span>, and (ii) <span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Factor-first</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">A greedy sampler mistakenly favors path (i) because the binary digits of <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> exhibit lower per-token uncertainty (requiring a choice only from <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>) than the decimal digits of <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> (which have 10 possible values). As shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, by minimizing immediate uncertainty, the greedy strategy commits to a product without fixing the factors, leading to incorrect equations and high residual uncertainty. Conversely, an optimal strategy would resolve the higher-uncertainty factors <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> first; once fixed, <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> can be determined with nearly zero uncertainty. Empirically, the greedy certainty-based sampler (represented by Entropy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) prioritizes path (i) with 73.2% probability, leading to significantly higher cumulative uncertainty.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Case Study 2 : Binary Judgment.</span>
In this experiment, the model is tasked with judging the truth of an arithmetic statement using the template: “[reasoning-masks] The answer is (Yes/No): [answer-mask]”. The answer token typically exhibits lower local uncertainty as it is constrained to a binary choice (Yes/No), whereas the reasoning steps involve much higher uncertainty. Consequently, greedy samplers tend to decode the answer token prematurely, making a commitment before the underlying reasoning is resolved. This leads to incorrect judgments and leaves high residual uncertainty in the reasoning positions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To analyze this, we compare greedy certainty-based samplers against an auto-regressive (AR) baseline, which naturally resolves high-uncertainty reasoning before the binary answer. As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Motivation ‣ 3 Method ‣ Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the AR baseline achieves superior accuracy and lower cumulative uncertainty, highlighting that greedy MDM samplers fail by prematurely committing to low-uncertainty answer tokens before the reasoning is established.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Quantitative results for Case Study 2.</span></figcaption>
